prompt: A sorted array of 1,000,000 user IDs needs at most 20 binary-search probes to find an ID or conclude it is absent. The user base grows to 2,000,000 IDs. What happens to the worst-case number of probes?

options.explanation: That would be true of a linear scan, whose cost grows in proportion to the array size. Binary search halves the range at every probe.

options.text: It stays at 20, because binary search is constant-time
options.explanation: Binary search is fast but not constant-time: a larger array needs more halvings to reach a single candidate.

options.text: It roughly quadruples, as for a quadratic algorithm
options.explanation: Nothing in binary search compares every pair. Its cost grows with the logarithm of the size, the slowest-growing cost in this list.

options.text: It goes up by one, to 21
options.explanation: Correct. The first probe of the larger array halves it back to about a million candidates, after which the search behaves exactly as before. Doubling the data adds one probe; a billion IDs need only 30.

workedExample:
Halve until one element remains:

```
2,000,000 -> 1,000,000 (probe 1)
1,000,000 -> 500,000 -> ...
   (about 20 more halvings)
```

1. A million candidates take at most 20 probes: 2 to the power 20 is just over a million.
2. Two million candidates need one extra halving first, so at most 21 probes.
3. Each doubling adds one probe: a billion IDs need about 30.

That logarithmic growth is why binary search scales so well, as long as the data stays sorted.
